source.suraNameGloss: The Moon (sura name; not translated as content)
source.primary_manuscript: Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BnF Arabe 328 + St. Petersburg, National Library of Russia, Marcel 18 / 13 et al. + Birmingham, Cadbury Research Library Mingana 1572a + Vatican, BAV Vat. ar. 1605/1 fragments)
source.primary_manuscript_dating: Hijazi script; late 7th century CE — radiocarbon analyses of Mingana 1572a (one of the dispersed fragments of this codex) by the Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit yielded a 95.4% probability range of 568–645 CE (Birmingham Qur'an radiocarbon study, 2015), placing this manuscript among the earliest-known Qur'anic witnesses; the broader codex-Parisino-petropolitanus body is conventionally dated to the late 7th century CE on palaeographic grounds (Déroche 2009).
source.primary_manuscript_script: Hijazi (slanted mā'il style; characteristic late-7th-c. CE early Quranic ductus)
source.primary_manuscript_contains: Approximately 45% of the Qur'an across the dispersed fragments; includes Suras 53–56 in a continuous run preserved primarily in BnF Arabe 328a folios.
source.cross_collation_manuscript: Sanʿāʾ 1 palimpsest (the lower text C-1; Yemen, Dar al-Makhtutat — but this manuscript does NOT preserve Sura 54 in the lower text per Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 §4 catalogue; the cross-collation is consulted only for orthographic-norm comparison, not for variant readings at Sura 54:1)
source.reference_vocalization: Cairo 1924 King Fuad edition (Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim reading-tradition) — the standard printed Qur'an.
source.transliteration_convention: DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) scientific transliteration: ʾ for hamza, ʿ for ʿayn, ḥ for ḥāʾ, ṭ ḍ ṣ ẓ for emphatic consonants, ġ for ghayn, ḫ for khāʾ, ṯ for thāʾ, ḏ for dhāl, š for shīn, macrons for long vowels.
source.verificationStatus: best-effort reconstruction; verification pending against the BnF original codicology (Arabe 328a), the Déroche 2009 facsimile-edition apparatus, the Birmingham Mingana 1572a 2015 radiocarbon-report appendix, and the Corpus Coranicum digital comparative apparatus. The rasm for Sura 54:1 is well-attested and stable across the early Hijazi witnesses; the Cairo Hafs reading supplied as the reference vocalization is the late-medieval crystallization of the dominant reading-tradition.
source.fetchedFrom: Corpus Coranicum digital apparatus (corpuscoranicum.de) for the rasm-skeleton and variant apparatus; Tanzil.net Cairo Hafs text for the reference vocalization; Déroche 2009 + Sadeghi-Bergmann 2010 for codicological framing; the Birmingham 2015 radiocarbon-report for the Mingana 1572a dating.
source.citation: Déroche, François, La transmission écrite du Coran dans les débuts de l'islam: le codex Parisino-petropolitanus (Brill 2009); Déroche, François, Qur'ans of the Umayyads (Brill 2014); Sadeghi, Behnam, and Bergmann, Uwe, 'The Codex of a Companion of the Prophet and the Qurʾān of the Prophet' (Arabica 57, 2010); Sadeghi, Behnam, and Goudarzi, Mohsen, 'Sanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān' (Der Islam 87, 2010); Hilali, Asma, The Sanaa Palimpsest (Oxford 2017); Birmingham Qur'an radiocarbon report (University of Birmingham + Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit, 2015, on Mingana 1572a); Neuwirth, Angelika, Scripture, Poetry, and the Making of a Community (Oxford 2014); Reynolds, Gabriel Said (ed.), The Qur'ān in Its Historical Context (Routledge 2008/2011); Corpus Coranicum project (BBAW, Berlin); Tanzil.net.
source.paleography_note: The `rasm` field provides the consonantal skeleton without vowel marks (tashkīl). Letter-discrimination dots (iʿjām) are absent in the Codex Parisino-petropolitanus rasm for the families of letters that share an identical skeletal shape (the *bāʾ / tāʾ / thāʾ / nūn / yāʾ* group; the *fāʾ / qāf* pair; the *dāl / dhāl* pair; the *rāʾ / zāy* pair; the *sīn / shīn* pair; the *ṣād / ḍād* pair; the *ṭāʾ / ẓāʾ* pair; the *ʿayn / ghayn* pair; the *jīm / ḥāʾ / khāʾ* group). The `rasm_paleography_note` field on the ayah documents which specific letters would appear without their dots in the manuscript. Hamza was not marked in the earliest Hijazi manuscripts and is omitted from the rasm where the underlying carrier-letter convention allows. Word-final tāʾ marbūṭa (ة) was written as undifferentiated hāʾ (ه) in the earliest manuscripts.
source.rasmConventionNote: Rasm rendered as: tashkīl-stripped, hamza-glyphs collapsed to underlying carrier, tāʾ-marbūṭa rendered as hāʾ. Letter-shapes preserved as modern codepoints, with the `rasm_paleography_note` documenting which letters are affected by the absence of iʿjām dots.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters in Codex Parisino-petropolitanus: *qāf* of اقتربت and of القمر (dotless ڡ-skeleton — fāʾ/qāf are visually identical in Hijazi rasm, with the upper double-dot of qāf and single-dot of fāʾ being a later addition); *tāʾ* of اقتربت (×2 — both medial and final positions show single-tooth skeletons; the final tāʾ here is the 'open' tāʾ tāʾ-maftūḥa, written as ت rather than ة because it is part of the verbal-inflection -at suffix); *bāʾ* of اقتربت (medial single-tooth, indistinguishable from t/th/n/y); *sīn* of الساعه (toothed three-tooth skeleton; without the upper three dots that would identify it as shīn it could be confused with shīn in the rasm); *ʿayn* of الساعه (lower bowl-form already dotless in dotted manuscripts; here unambiguous since ghayn would have an upper dot which is absent in rasm — so the reader must rely on lexical knowledge to distinguish saʿa from saġa); *nūn* of وانشق (medial single-tooth indistinguishable from b/t/th/y); *shīn* of وانشق (toothed three-tooth skeleton without the upper three dots that distinguish shīn from sīn — in the rasm a reader cannot visually distinguish *inshaqqa* 'split' from a hypothetical *insaqqa*). **CRITICAL PALEOGRAPHIC FACT**: the word ٱنشق 'has split' in this ayah is in the rasm visually identical to a sequence that could in principle be read as ٱنسق — the lexical disambiguation is provided by the recitation-tradition and by the *iʿjām* dots added in later centuries. In practice no scribal or recitation variant has been recorded that reads this ayah differently from *inshaqqa l-qamaru*; the rasm-skeleton's ambiguity is theoretical, not practical. The *q* of القمر is the second of two qāf-skeletons in this short ayah (the first being in اقتربت). **TĀʾ-MARBŪṬA**: الساعه is written with a final hāʾ-shape (ه) in the early manuscripts, becoming الساعة (with tāʾ-marbūṭa ة dots) only in the 8th–9th century scribal reform.
ayahs.notes: **MAJOR THEME — the splitting-of-the-moon (inshiqāq al-qamar) eschatological sign.** The opening ayah of Sūrat al-Qamar (sura 54). The verb *iqtarabati* (Form VIII of q-r-b 'to be near') is the same form that opens Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ (21:1, iqtaraba li-n-nāsi); the structural parallel (the only two suras in the Qurʾān that open with this verb) is foregrounded in classical tafsīr as deliberate stylistic resonance (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī). The *sāʿa* 'the Hour' is the technical Quranic eschatological term for the Day of Judgment / end of the world (cf. 6:31, 7:187, 12:107, 15:85, 16:77, 18:21, 18:36, 19:75, 20:15, 21:49, 22:1, 22:7, 22:55, 25:11, 30:12, 30:14, 30:55, 31:34, 33:63, 34:3, 40:46, 40:59, 41:47, 41:50, 42:17, 42:18, 43:61, 43:66, 43:85, 45:27, 45:32, 47:18, 54:1, 54:46, 79:42 — the term occurs 49 times). The verb *inshaqqa* (Form VII of š-q-q 'to split/cleave') is in the perfect aspect ('has split'); the classical exegetical tradition (al-Ṭabarī's Jāmiʿ al-bayān) divides over whether this describes a past event (the so-called *shaqq al-qamar* miracle attributed to Muḥammad in Mecca, recorded in Bukhārī, Muslim, and the *sīra*-tradition: Ibn Hishām, Ibn Saʿd, al-Wāqidī) or a future eschatological sign (the moon's splitting as a portent of the Hour). The mainstream Sunni tradition reads it as both — past historical sign + eschatological foreshadowing. **HIGHEST RAËLIAN-CANON LENS-RISK SITE IN THIS TRANSLATION**: in *Extra-Terrestrials Took Me To Their Planet* (Raël 1977), this ayah is read **literally** as a description of an Elohim-spacecraft / atomic-propulsion event that physically split the moon — the canon presents this as evidence of pre-modern (7th-c.) observation of ET technology. This is the canon's most explicit 'the Qurʾān describes ET tech' citation. **Operational disavowal required in the apparatus**: acknowledge-without-endorse pattern (same as the Shi'ur Qomah parasangs precedent); name the canon's reading explicitly and route it through named-scholarship attribution rather than adopting the reading. Cross-corpus: cf. Joel 2:30-31 / Acts 2:19-20 ('I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke; the sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come'); cf. Matt 24:29 / Mark 13:24-25 ('the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven'); cf. Rev 6:12-13 ('there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black ... and the moon became as blood'); cf. Isa 13:10, Isa 24:23, Ezek 32:7-8 (the prophetic-tradition cosmic-portent corpus). The Quranic *inshiqāq al-qamar* sits within this Near-Eastern apocalyptic moon-darkening / moon-blood / moon-splitting tradition. **Modern scientific note**: the 1968-1972 Apollo missions found no geological evidence of moon-splitting; the literal-Quranic moon-split apologetic position (popular among 20th-c. Islamic apologists like Zakir Naik) is rejected by mainstream geology. The mainstream exegetical position remains the past-miracle reading (Bukhārī 4:60:387; Muslim 39:6717) plus eschatological-foreshadowing reading. **PALEOGRAPHY**: this ayah opens Sūrat al-Qamar; in Codex Parisino-petropolitanus it would be preceded by a basmala and possibly a decorative band; the sura-name is not written in the earliest manuscripts.
ayahs.variants: No major rasm-level variants attested between Codex Parisino-petropolitanus and other early Hijazi witnesses for this ayah; the consonantal skeleton is stable. The Cairo Hafs reading *iqtarabati s-sāʿatu wa-nšaqqa l-qamaru* is also the reading of the Warsh ʿan Nāfiʿ and other major canonical reading-traditions. Classical *qirāʾāt* literature records no significant variant for this ayah (cf. Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī l-qirāʾāt; al-Dānī, Kitāb al-Taysīr). The orthographic question of whether السَّاعَة was written الساعه (final hāʾ) or الساعة (final tāʾ-marbūṭa) in the original Hijazi manuscript is a scribal-development question, not a textual variant: the dots distinguishing tāʾ-marbūṭa from hāʾ were added in the 8th–9th century reform.
